1: Welcome to the story deck for Building Ticket-to-Machine, a developer workbook in the Federal Modernization Workbook.
Instead of eight chapters one at a time, we'll follow one person's record all the way through Book 13's loop on ServiceNow and SailPoint.
Her name is Erin, and she's fictional: every value you'll see comes from the kit's own test fixtures, and every command was re-run before it went on a slide.

Seven scenes: the drift run finds her, her drift becomes a typed task, least-privilege clients touch it, we find why it keeps coming back, the fix is actuated, a re-read closes it, and her closure becomes evidence an I S S O can verify.
Each scene ends with a command to try and a one-question check.
One more thing before we start: the code is illustrative.
Its tests pass against fixtures and mocked responses, but it hasn't been run against a live ServiceNow instance or SailPoint tenant.
Where the vendors' documentation doesn't settle a point, the workbook says so, and so will we.

Entra I D, in a Microsoft 365 G C C tenant, says Finance, and a different manager.

H R agreeing later doesn't make a hand-typed change authorized, so a person decides it.
Each of Erin's findings becomes one typed task in ServiceNow: a class, a severity, the system where it'll be re-read, one subject, its origin, and the intended state a re-read must find.
Her department drift is P3, due in a day.
The unauthorized write is P2, due in an hour, and it's accepted with a warning, because its intended state is empty until that person decides.
From SailPoint's side, the mover workflow raises her department change with Finance as the intended state.
Why it matters: Gate 4 makes every drift an owned record answered inside a window.
The tempo is Book 13's design, not a federal clock.
The important design choice is that the rules liv in one place, the scripted REST resource inside ServiceNow, and the Python mirror is held to it by a test that reads the JavaScript.
So a malformed payload fails on a laptop, not as a four hundred from a live instance, and the mirror can't quietly go stale.

Scene three: who may touch Erin's record.
The drift client read her through SailPoint with two read scopes, and through Graph with the user read permission plus the audit permission.
That audit read is the only reason the help desk write was seen.
In ServiceNow, a finding writer posted her tasks, only the verifier may close them, and an evidence reader may only read.
Every call is a row in one file, and a test fails on any call it doesn't declare.
Why it matters: Gate 1 records the integration identities, each least-privileged, with certificates rather than secrets, and the closer separated from the raisers.
Two details from Chapter 3 are worth carrying.
A SailPoint client-credentials token has no user context, and SailPoint warns that most admin A P I's often return forbidden with one, so Lab 2 records what actually works in your sandbox.
And the scope that creates workflows lives on its own client, used once, then removed.

17: The kit's provisioning fixture is Alice's, not Erin's, but the shape is the same for anyone.
Resolve SailPoint's provisioning-completed workflow against it.
ServiceNow gets a closure signal, accepted, with four input fields not sent.
And here's what a closure signal does: it moves matching findings to awaiting verification.
That's the example guide's first gap, written into code: a success response is not closure.
The workflow is also why provisioning status can't be trusted on its own.
SailPoint's own best-practice page says its Service Desk integration treats the mapped ServiceNow status as completion.
The kit turns that around: a status or a success only starts the wait for evidence.

22: The answer to check six: no.
Resolved is a lead; only a matching re-read closes the record.
When the re-read verified Erin's record, it wrote the result with an evidence hash.
On a real instance, that closed record is read back out and written as one line of an evidence package, in Book 13's shape: origin, owner and clock, the re-read result, and the closure.
Approval, the executing identity and what ran are written as null, each with its reason, because the first pass doesn't actuate.
The record says what it doesn't hold.
Each line carries the hash of the line before it, and a manifest holds a hash of every file.
The I S S O gets records nobody could edit or remove without it showing.

The file's hash no longer matches the manifest, and the next line's link is broken.
Next month's export continues the chain from this month's manifest, so a gap between periods shows too.
One limit to remember: the package is tamper-evident, not signed.
Someone who can rewrite every file and the manifest can rewrite the chain, so keep each manifest where the exporter can't write.
